(a) Definitions.—In this section:
        (1) Park.—The term “Park” means the Virgin Islands National Park. 
        (2) Resort.—The term “resort” means the Caneel Bay resort on the island of St. John in the Park. 
        (3) Retained use estate.—The term “retained use estate” means the retained use estate for the Caneel Bay property on the island of St. John entered into between the Jackson Hole Preserve and the United States on September 30, 1983 (as amended, assigned, and assumed). 
        (4) Secretary.—The term “Secretary” means the Secretary of the Interior.  
    (b) Lease Authorization.—
        (1) In general.—If the Secretary determines that the long-term benefit to the Park would be greater by entering into a lease with the owner of the retained use estate than by authorizing a concession contract upon the termination of the retained use estate, the Secretary may enter into a lease with the owner of the retained use estate for the operation and management of the resort. 
        (2) Acquisitions.—The Secretary may—
            (A) acquire associated property from the owner of the retained use estate; and 
            (B) on the acquisition of property under subparagraph (A), administer the property as part of the Park.  
        (3) Authority.—Except as otherwise provided by this section, a lease shall be in accordance with subsection (k) of section 3 of Public Law 91–383 (16 U.S.C. 1a–2(k)), notwithstanding paragraph (2) of that subsection. 
        (4) Terms and conditions.—A lease authorized under this section shall—
            (A) be for the minimum number of years practicable, taking into consideration the need for the lessee to secure financing for necessary capital improvements to the resort, but in no event shall the term of the lease exceed 40 years; 
            (B) prohibit any transfer, assignment, or sale of the lease or otherwise convey or pledge any interest in the 
lease without prior written notification to, and approval by the Secretary; 
            (C) ensure that the general character of the resort property remains unchanged, including a prohibition against—
                (i) any increase in the overall size of the resort; or 
                (ii) any increase in the number of guest accommodations available at the resort;  
            (D) prohibit the sale of partial ownership shares or timeshares in the resort; 
            (E) include provisions to ensure the protection of the natural, cultural, and historic features of the resort and associated property, consistent with the laws and policies applicable to property managed by the National Park Service; and 
            (F) include any other provisions determined by the Secretary to be necessary to protect the Park and the public interest.  
        (5) Rental amounts.—In determining the fair market value rental of the lease required under section 3(k)(4) of Public Law 91–383 (16 U.S.C. 1a–2(k)(4)), the Secretary shall take into consideration—
            (A) the value of any associated property conveyed to the United States; and 
            (B) the value, if any, of the relinquished term of the retained use estate.  
        (6) Use of proceeds.—Rental amounts paid to the United States under a lease shall be available to the Secretary, without further appropriation, for visitor services and resource protection within the Park. 
        (7) Congressional notification.—The Secretary shall submit a proposed lease under this section to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources of the Senate and the Committee on Natural Resources of the House of Representatives at least 60 days before the award of the lease. 
        (8) Renewal.—A lease entered into under this section may not be extended or renewed. 
        (9) Termination.—Upon the termination of a lease entered into under this section, if the Secretary determines the continuation of commercial services at the resort to be appropriate, the services shall be provided in accordance with the National Park Service Concessions Management Improvement Act of 1998 (16 U.S.C. 5951 et seq.).  
    (c) Retained Use Estate.—
        (1) In general.—As a condition of the lease, the owner of the retained use estate shall terminate, extinguish, and relinquish to the Secretary all rights under the retained use estate and shall transfer, without consideration, ownership of improvements on the retained use estate to the National Park Service. 
        (2) Appraisal.—
            (A) In general.—The Secretary shall require an appraisal by an independent, qualified appraiser who is agreed to by the Secretary and the owner of the retained use estate to determine the value, if any, of the relinquished term of the retained use estate. 
            (B) Requirements.—An appraisal under paragraph (1) shall be conducted in accordance with—
                (i) the Uniform Appraisal Standards for Federal Land Acquisitions; and 
                (ii) the Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice.

fable.w: The tempting reading treats the 60-day submission of the proposed lease, or the appraiser 'agreed to by the Secretary and the owner', as outside participation. The submission goes only to congressional committees, which are inside the federal government. The lease and the jointly agreed appraiser are terms of a bilateral property transaction with the private counterparty, closer to a contract than to consultation on a federal policy decision. The section has no public comment, hearing, rulemaking, advisory body, or right to sue.
fable.s: The Secretary shall submit a proposed lease under this section to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources of the Senate and the Committee on Natural Resources of the House of Representatives at least 60 days before the award of the lease.

qwen_block.w: The section primarily authorizes the Secretary to enter into a lease with a private entity and requires notification to Congress. Congress is inside the federal government, so notification to it is not participation. The interaction with the private owner is a bilateral contractual negotiation (including agreeing on an appraiser), which falls under the exclusion for contracts/applications rather than participatory processes like public hearings, advisory boards, or mandatory consultation with outside entities on policy decisions.
qwen_block.s: The Secretary shall submit a proposed lease under this section to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources of the Senate and the Committee on Natural Resources of the House of Representatives at least 60 days before the award of the lease.
qwen_block.b:
1. **Think briefly**: The section describes a process where the Secretary of the Interior may enter into a lease with the owner of a retained use estate (a private entity, "Jackson Hole Preserve"). It includes a requirement for "Congressional notification" (subsection b(7)), which is a trap because Congress is inside the federal government. However, the core action is the Secretary entering into a lease with a private owner. Does this constitute "participation" as defined? The definition says participation is when the government consults or coordinates with people *outside* the government *before* making a decision. Entering into a lease is a decision/action. Is there consultation? Subsection (c)(2) requires an appraisal by an appraiser "agreed to by the Secretary and the owner". This is a form of coordination/consultation with an outside party (the owner) regarding the valuation, which is part of the lease decision. More importantly, the definition includes "consultation or coordination with... companies... before a federal action". The lease itself is a federal action involving a private company. However, looking at the "No" traps: "applications for benefits, grants, contracts, or licenses - applying for something is not participating in the decision". A lease is a contract. Is the *process* of negotiating the lease considered participation? The definition emphasizes *consultation* or *coordination*. The text says the Secretary *may* enter into a lease if they determine it's beneficial. It doesn't explicitly mandate a public comment period or an advisory board. But wait, look at Example 2: "consultation and coordination with appropriate State and local governmental agencies... may allow a nongovernmental organization to serve...". Here, the Secretary coordinates with the owner to agree on an appraiser. Is that enough? Let's look closer. The definition says "Participation is when the federal government may or must consult or coordinate with people outside of the government before making a decision." The agreement on the appraiser is a coordination step before the final valuation/lease terms are set. Also, the lease terms are negotiated with the owner. Negotiation is a form of coordination. However, many contract negotiations are not considered "participation" in the regulatory sense. Let's re-read the "No" traps carefully. "Applications for... contracts... is not participating". This is a lease authorization. The Secretary *decides* whether to lease. The owner *applies* or is the existing holder. The text doesn't say the Secretary *must* consult the public or an advisory board. It says the Secretary *may* enter into a lease. The only interaction with an outsider is the negotiation of the lease terms and the agreement on an appraiser. Is agreement on an appraiser "consultation/coordination before making a decision"? Yes, it's a procedural step involving an outsider. But is it the *kind* of participation the definition targets? The definition targets things like advisory boards, comment periods, hearings. Example 11 says an opportunity to present views in an enforcement context is "No". Example 9 says consultation *within* a state plan submission is "No". Here, the coordination is between the Federal agency and the private owner regarding the lease. This is essentially a bilateral negotiation. Is bilateral negotiation "participation"? Usually, "participation" implies a broader or more formalized input mechanism (like a board or public comment). However, the definition is broad: "consult or coordinate... before making a decision". The agreement on the appraiser is a specific coordination requirement. Let's look for a stronger signal. There is no public comment period. There is no advisory board. There is no consultation with states/tribes. The only outsider is the leaseholder. The interaction is contractual. In Example 5, an agreement with a union was "No" because it was past tense. Here, the lease is future. But is it participation? The definition excludes "applications for... contracts". This is the execution of a contract. I lean towards "No" because the interaction is purely bilateral contractual negotiation, not a participatory process like a hearing or advisory committee. The "agreement on an appraiser" is a standard contractual clause, not a participatory governance mechanism. The "Congressional notification" is a trap (No). The rest is internal decision-making or bilateral contract terms.

Wait, let's look at Example 10. An advisory board determines emblems. That's "Yes". Example 4. A commission with outside members. "Yes". Example 2. Consultation with states/tribes. "Yes".
Does this section have an advisory board? No.
Does it have a public hearing? No.
Does it have consultation with states/tribes? No.
Does it have a right to sue? No.
Does it have a comment period? No.
The only potential is the "agreement on an appraiser". Is that "consultation"? It's a mutual agreement. Is it "participation"? The definition says "consult or coordinate". Mutual agreement is coordination. But is it the *type* of participation intended? The "No" trap for contracts suggests that the mere existence of a contract negotiation isn't participation. The definition focuses on *input* into a decision. The owner's input is their offer/negotiation. This is standard commerce, not "participation" in the administrative law sense usually captured by these labels (which focus on democratic or expert input). I will label "No".

Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the requirement to agree on an appraiser with the owner constitutes "coordination with a person outside the government before making a decision" (the valuation/lease). However, this is a standard contractual provision for valuation, not a participatory process like a public hearing or advisory committee. The definition's exclusion of "applications for... contracts" suggests that bilateral contractual negotiations are not the target. The primary interaction is the Secretary's unilateral determination of benefit, followed by a contract. The congressional notification is internal.

The proposed lease goes only to congressional committees, which are inside the federal government. Reading the joint appraiser selection as participation would treat a technical step in a lease deal as public input; no hearing, comment period, advisory body or right to sue is created.

opus.b:
I labelled this **No**, with moderate confidence (0.68). The section authorizes the Secretary to lease the Caneel Bay resort to its current owner, and nothing in it brings outsiders into a federal decision.

- **Congressional notification (paragraph (b)(7)):** This is the most procedural-looking part, but it is a notice to Senate and House committees. Congress is inside the federal government, so it doesn't count.
- **The owner's role:** The owner of the retained use estate deals with the Secretary as a party to the lease. It negotiates terms, gives up its rights, and transfers ownership of its improvements. That is entering into a contract, which the definition excludes, not taking part in a public decision.
- **The appraisal (paragraph (c)(2)):** This is the closest call. The Secretary and the owner must jointly agree on the independent appraiser. Read broadly, that gives an outside party a say in a federal decision. I treated it as No because it only sets up a technical valuation within the lease deal. There is no comment period, hearing, advisory body or right to sue. A stricter reading could count the joint selection as participation, which is why my confidence is not higher.

Congressional notification is not participation because Congress is inside the federal government. The interaction with the private owner is contractual (leasing) rather than consultative in the sense of seeking advice or coordination before a policy decision. The appraisal process is a valuation step for the transaction, not a participatory governance mechanism.
